info.bio:
Punk y hard rock artista: Billy Idol (William Michael Albert Broad, n. 30 de noviembre de 1955 en Middlesex, Inglaterra) es un músico inglés de rock.

Idol vivió en Worthing antes de acudir a la Universidad de Sussex, solamente un año, antes de unirse al Bromley Contingent, formado por fans de los Sex Pistols. Durante este período, Idol decidió convertirse en músico, y formó su propia banda, Generation X, en 1976. Además, se convirtió en vegetariano porque quería parecerse a David Bowie.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los ochenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Absorbida la new wave, el mundo de los cantautores no vuelve a ser el mismo: los referentes pasan a ser Dylan, Neil Young, Cohen, Tim Buckley y Joni Mitchell. Las mujeres recuperan su estatus de seres filosóficos: Phranc, Suzanne Vega, Tracy Chapman, Melissa Etheridge, Michelle Shocked, Barbara Manning, Lucinda y Victoria Williams, Indigo Girls y, en Canadá, Jane Siberry, Mary Margaret O'Hara y Sarah McLachlan. Excéntricos: Jandek, Daniel Johnston, David Thomas, Alejandro Escovedo; en California, Stan Ridgway, Chris Isaak y Smog. En Gran Bretaña, Billy Bragg, Robyn Hitchcock, Julian Cope y, la voz más importante de la década, Nick Cave, predicador del apocalipsis moral (From Her To Eternity, The Good Son). Sinéad O'Connor, Sting, Morrissey, Momus; el pop celta de Enya y Loreena McKennitt; al cambiar la década, Joe Henry, Daniel Lanois y Bob Mould.

podcast.title: "I Want My MTV" Campaign
podcast.body: Billy Idol was one of the prominent artists who appeared in promos for the "I Want My MTV" campaign. This highly effective campaign encouraged people to call their local cable companies to demand that they carry the new channel, significantly expanding MTV's reach and power across the US. "Promos like this began to run constantly on MTV featuring the police, Pat Benatar, Pete Townsend, Cindy Loper, Billy Eidle, and even David Bowie."

podcast.title: Audience Chant for "Mony Mony"
podcast.body: Billy Idol's live performances of "Mony Mony" are famous for an obscene audience call-and-response chant where listeners respond to "here she comes now singing Moni Moni" with phrases like "hey, mother F, get late, get F'd." This phenomenon, documented with regional variations (Toronto, Denver, Texas), emerged spontaneously around 1987, spreading intercontinentally without the internet, radio, or music videos. "The audience responds with some version of the following, hey, mother F, get late, get F'd."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Endorsement of Audience Chant (Late 80s)
podcast.body: Billy Idol endorsed the obscene audience chant for "Mony Mony" during one of the first documented occasions of its use at the Mandalay Bay Hotel in Las Vegas in the late 1980s. "One of the first documented occasions of the crowd chant was at the Mandalay Bay Hotel in Las Vegas in the late 80s, an occasion during which Billy endorsed the lyrics himself."

podcast.title: Influenced by The Ramones
podcast.body: Billy Idol saw The Ramones perform in England in 1976 and was deeply impressed, finding them "brilliant." This experience directly influenced how his band, Generation X, chose to play. "Billy Idol said he thought they were brilliant and it influenced how his band chose to play."

podcast.title: John Hughes Film Exposure (1980s)
podcast.body: Billy Idol's music was heavily featured on the carefully selected soundtracks of John Hughes' 1980s films. These soundtracks served as a significant platform for exposing many people, particularly in North America, to various alternative rock bands, especially those originating from the UK. "So many people learned of bands like The Specials and Spandovalet and Billy Idle and General Public and Wang Chung and Yellow and New Order and the Psychedelic Furs and the Smiths and Echo and the Bunyman, Susanne Vagan in excess the Jesus and Mary chain, Flesh for Luluo and so many others from those soundtrack albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Las Vegas Residency Trend
podcast.body: Billy Idol was among the rock bands that started accepting offers for Las Vegas residencies, a growing trend in the 21st century. This move allowed artists to perform to fans in a fixed location, avoiding the arduous demands of continuous touring. "David Lee Roth, Error Smith, Motley Crude, Journey, The Eagles, and Billy Idle among them."

podcast.title: Origin of Chant (Billy Idol's Theory)
podcast.body: Billy Idol heard that the "Mony Mony" audience chant originated in London's fraternity houses in the 1980s. He theorized that it then "graduated to the Disco's and then the DJ's would start shouting it" before eventually making its way to live shows. "Well, I heard it was started off in London's Fratt Houses back in the 80s, I suppose, that the Fratt House started it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Personal Connection to "Mony Mony"
podcast.body: Billy Idol revealed in an MTV interview and his autobiography, "Dancing with Myself," that the original Tommy James song "Mony Mony" was playing on the radio the night he lost his virginity. "During an MTV interview, Billy said the song was playing on the radio the night he lost his virginity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Punk Scene Roots
podcast.body: Born William Broad, Billy Idol was deeply immersed in the original punk rock scene, actively following the Sex Pistols and associating with seminal figures like Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious before adopting his stage name and forming Generation X. "William Broad followed the pistols everywhere. He was deep into the original punk rock scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rejected "Don't You (Forget About Me)"
podcast.body: Billy Idol was approached to record the song "Don't You (Forget About Me)" for *The Breakfast Club* soundtrack but ultimately turned it down. The song was initially written by Keith Forsey with Brian Ferry in mind, and after Idol's rejection, it eventually found its way to Simple Minds, becoming their biggest hit. "Then Forsy approached Billy Idle to record the song for the movie. He turned it down."

xref.title: Billy Idol Witnesses The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
xref.body: A "very young Billy Isle" (Idol), then part of Generation X, was present at The Ramones' influential gig at the Roundhouse in London on July 4, 1976. He was among the many future British punk figures who were "transformed by what they saw and heard." "Generation X featuring a very young Billy Isle. They were all at these gigs and they were all transformed by what they saw and heard."

xref.title: Bromley Contingent – Fan Group
xref.body: The band had a dedicated group of fans known as the Bromley Contingent, which included notable future artists such as Sid Vicious, Billy Idol, and Siouxsie Sioux. "He was a member of a group of fans called the Bromley Contingent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Catalyst for British Punk Explosion
xref.body: The Ramones' two London gigs in July 1976 are considered foundational for the British punk rock explosion. Major figures like Johnny Rotten, Sid Vicious, Joe Strummer, Chrissy Hynde, The Damned, and Billy Idol were in attendance and were profoundly "transformed by what they saw and heard," inspiring them to form their own bands. "Over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sex Pistols' Number One Fan – Bromley Contingent Member
xref.body: Sid was the Sex Pistols' biggest fan and a member of the "Bromley Contingent," a group of dedicated followers that also included future stars like Billy Idol and Siouxsie Sioux. He followed the band everywhere. "Sid became the Sex Pistols number one fan."
